The term RSI is ~20 years old at this point, and the concept is even older. If an AI can't continuously modify itself and instead has to build a successor that builds a successor, that changes some specifics (for example, the alignment problem becomes more relevant - how can the AI ensure that its successor shares its goals?) but it's still a situation that may produce exponential growth, and hence most RSI-related considerations still apply.

(In fact, as a toy example, note that it's in theory possible to get exponential growth in capabilities even if you hold the software fixed, if e.g. you have an AI that can design and build better hardware to run itself faster on, which lets it design even better hardware even faster.)

My initial knee-jerk reaction was to list out a whole bunch of reasons why this take is wrong, or shortsighted, or gives too much credit to LLMs as a “revolution”, or any of the other go-tos in my satchel of counterpoints to the usual ad nauseam AI discourse.

Except those don’t really fit, here, because the author is making a far more critical error in ascribing far too much to current human cognition. On the daily I see so-called “knowledge workers” failing to read basic signs, refusing to learn basic skills, and all too eager to cast off the slightest bit of critical thinking to a black box they can subscribe to - be it replacing curating a content library with streaming services and algorithms, or swapping a life of hard-won expertise for a swarm of chatbots and an API bucket. As someone with the uniquely privileged POV to be able to ingest vast sums of technical data but struggle with social data, I look at my fellow Americans and genuinely fret for what the next few decades hold for a cohort that seemingly cannot effectively communicate which direction they’re going but is all too content to hitch their accountability to an LLM they pay for.

In that sense, thinking has already become a hobby to the masses, in that it’s entirely optional to exist in current society at large. Autopay apps manage your bills, finance apps keep you on budget, fitness apps tell you to keep running, social media apps tell you who your friends (and enemies) are, video apps tell you what to watch, music apps tell you what to listen to, and cars increasingly tell you not just where to go but also to let them get there for you. I would argue that in that context, thinking is a critically endangered hobby we sorely need to sow new seeds for, lest we risk losing it entirely; AI does not seem keen to do that.

Now to be fair, so much of this is hyperspecialization knowledge overflowing into daily life and making existence a sort of cognitohazard in and of itself. We skip through hundreds of pages of legal boilerplate because we’re not lawyers, and then complain about all the rights we willingly signed away because of the volume of said agreements. Non-technical people engaging with modern computing are either addicts or miserable, unaware that this was both entirely optional and also inevitable in a populace that didn’t think for itself. Finance has become so hyperspecialized that it’s impossible for the layman to tell of something is good or bad, or even why the number went up or down on their portfolio in a given time period. LLM boosters say their tools will solve this complexity nightmare, yet the tools themselves grow increasingly complex just to eke out single-point gains on hyperspecific problems.

Which brings me to the OP again, their highly uncritical claims that AI will bring about a new revolution of thought itself, and that somehow this tool will both restore thought to an elevated pedestal while also making it nearly impossible to meter (at least on American currency; let’s not think too hard about how developing countries might be able to afford it). I don’t see any of that, but for the same reasons the OP feels it’s somehow inevitable. The only difference I can readily figure is our opinions of our fellow humans: I view us as in dire straits and able to do far better than we give ourselves credit for, while they view us as replaceable with servile digital labor for the better.

VesiroSearch is a software that accelerates Elasticsearch query performance by up to 2x. The increase in search performance enables you to get by with up to 50% fewer server nodes, reducing costs considerably.

VesiroSearch is now in beta, which means that teams that run Elasticsearch can download and evaluate it using their own data and queries. The beta is free for the duration of our beta period for up to five nodes.

It installs as a standard plugin and the installation process takes about a minute. It doesn’t change the query DSL in Elasticsearch, which means that you do not have to change your queries or mappings to run it. No other end points are affected either, and VesiroSearch works with your current indices, so your setup remains the same.

VesiroSearch is a purpose-built C++ search engine that intercepts the query phase and executes it instead of the standard Elasticsearch.

The exact increase in performance depends on many variables such as query complexity, document size, number of documents, memory to index size ratio, etc. In customer pilots, we’ve consistently measured up to 2x faster search on indexes of up to several terabytes in size.

The improvement in search performance means that you need less CPU resources to handle the same search workload per given time unit. That enables you to do a few different things. If you change nothing you will be able to get much higher query throughput with your current server infrastructure. If you are looking to reduce costs, you can choose to reduce the number of server nodes until you get to the same level of query throughput you had before. You can also choose to move to cheaper server nodes.

This is mainly for teams running self-managed Elasticsearch clusters (on-prem or cloud doesn’t matter) at such a scale that cost has become an issue. The increase in search performance is useful if compute is part of your bottleneck. You can request access to run the beta version of the product. It’s free for the duration of our beta period for up to 5 nodes in total.

We would love to get feedback from teams that run Elasticsearch extensively. Learning which workloads that benefit from our acceleration, and which workloads we should add in our product roadmap would be super helpful. Also, if you have any feedback on compatibility or what would make evaluation easier, that would be greatly appreciated as well.

You can read more about the product here: https://vesiro.com And you can request access to the beta here: https://account.vesiro.com
